title: Translation Units, Linkage and Name Mangling
objectives: Trace how a program becomes translation units, object files and one linked binary, and predict where compile-time versus link-time errors originate
Apply the One Definition Rule to decide which declarations may be repeated across translation units and which must have exactly one definition
Control symbol visibility with internal linkage (static, anonymous namespaces, const objects) and read nm symbol tables (T/t/D/d/U)
Decode Itanium-ABI mangled names back to declarations and demangle them with nm -C and c++filt
Use extern "C" correctly to publish unmangled symbols for dlopen and ctypes boundaries
motivation: A desk ships one pricing library that gets compiled into the backtester, the risk engine and the execution gateway. One stray non-static global in a header turns tomorrow's build into a wall of 'multiple definition' errors, and a pricing function you want to call from Python through ctypes fails to load unless it is extern "C". None of this is about C++ syntax, it is about what the linker actually sees, and that is precisely what this lesson teaches you to inspect.

blocks.text: From source to binary: translation units

blocks.md: The compiler never sees your program. It sees one **translation unit** (TU) at a time: a single `.cpp` file after the preprocessor has pasted in every `#include` and expanded every macro. Anything not in that file, classes declared in a header, functions living in a library, is invisible; declarations are *promises* that the linker will later keep. Each TU compiles into an **object file** (`.o`) holding machine code plus a **symbol table**: symbols it defines (code and data that live here) and symbols it needs, marked undefined. The **linker** stitches object files and libraries together, resolving every undefined symbol against exactly one definition. This division of labour explains the two error families: compile errors mean a promise was broken inside one TU; link errors mean a promise was never kept anywhere.

blocks.caption: Three files, one program. Each .cpp is compiled blind to the others. Deliberate fragment; use the named surrounding files and definitions.

blocks.code:
g++ -c prices.cpp main.cpp
nm -C prices.o     # T mid_price()  - defined here
nm -C main.o       # U mid_price()  - needed from somewhere else
g++ main.o prices.o -o desk && ./desk
blocks.caption: Output: 42.17. The linker resolved the U against the T.

blocks.md: The ODR has two halves. A non-inline function or variable with **external linkage** must have **exactly one definition in the whole program**. Class definitions, inline functions and templates are different: they may be defined in *every* TU that uses them, but all those definitions must be **token-for-token identical**. Violating the repeatable half is ill-formed with no diagnostic required, the linker catches the blatant case (`multiple definition of ...`) but is structurally unable to catch the subtle one below.

blocks.title: The ODR break the linker cannot see
blocks.md: If `a.cpp` defines inline `double fee()` returning 0.02 and `b.cpp` defines inline `double fee()` returning 0.03, the program links cleanly: the linker assumes header-defined entities are identical. The optimiser inlines each TU's own version, so one part of the binary charges 0.02 and another 0.03. Keep reusable definitions in headers exactly once (single source of truth), and keep must-be-single definitions in .cpp files.

blocks.text: Linkage: who is allowed to see a name

blocks.md: A namespace-scope name has **external linkage** by default: it is visible to the linker and other TUs can refer to it. **Internal linkage** makes a name private to its TU. You get it three ways: `static` on a function or variable, membership of an anonymous `namespace {}`, and (a C++ quirk) `const` namespace-scope variables that are not declared `inline` or `extern`. Internal linkage prevents name collisions between TUs, keeps helpers out of your shared library's public symbol list, and gives the optimiser a guarantee that every use is in this file.

blocks.caption: The two anonymous 'anon' objects never clash. Two external 'visible' definitions would clash.

rows: defined here, in the code (text) section, external linkage
defined here, but local to this object file, internal linkage
defined here, initialised data, external linkage
undefined here, the linker must satisfy it from elsewhere
blocks.caption: Uppercase = external linkage, lowercase = internal. Only uppercase symbols participate in cross-TU linking.

blocks.md: C++ has namespaces and overloading, but linkers and C tooling understand only flat names. So the compiler **mangles**: it encodes namespace, name and parameter types into one symbol. Linux gcc and clang use the Itanium C++ ABI scheme: `_Z`, then the qualified name (`6square` = length 6 + 'square'; `N2fx5priceE` = nested fx::price), then the parameter types (`i` int, `d` double). Overloading works precisely because `square(int)` and `square(double)` get different symbols.

blocks.caption: Mangled symbols are an ABI detail, not a language guarantee, they differ between compilers.

blocks.code:
nm square.o                   # raw:        T _Z6squarei
nm -C square.o                # demangled:  T square(int)
c++filt _ZN2fx5priceEdi       # -> fx::price(double, int)
objdump -d square.o           # read the actual machine code
blocks.caption: The daily workflow: nm for symbols, c++filt or nm -C to translate, objdump to look inside.

blocks.md: `extern "C"` gives declarations **C language linkage**: the symbol is emitted unmangled and overloading is not allowed inside the block. It exists so that C code, Python's ctypes, Rust and `dlsym` can find functions by a plain string. Note what it does *not* do: it changes the name, not the type system, passing a `std::string` through an `extern "C"` function is still a cross-ABI risk, which is exactly where the next lessons go.

blocks.caption: extern "C" on the declaration is what makes the definition's symbol unmangled.

blocks.code: g++ -c bs.cpp && nm bs.o      # T bs_call  - no mangling, ready for dlsym/ctypes
blocks.caption: A plain name any foreign linker can resolve.

steps.note: T is defined here, U is a promise made to the linker
the promise was never kept: libm was not named on the command line
the linker only binds what you list: errors appear at link time, not compile time

blocks.caption: Compilation is private; linking is contractual. Every U symbol is a promise the final image must keep.

guidedExercise.prompt:
You run `g++ main.cpp compute.cpp && ./a.out; echo $?` where `compute.cpp` defines `int compute(int n) { return n * 2; }` and `main.cpp` contains only:

```cpp
int compute(int n);      // promise
int main() { return compute(21); }
```

Predict, before running anything: (1) the nm class of `compute` in `main.o` (T or U?), (2) the exact mangled symbol in `compute.o`, (3) the number `echo $?` prints.
hints: main.cpp has only a declaration, no body was compiled in that TU.
The Itanium mangling for a free function is _Z, then length+name, then parameter types.
On Linux the exit status of main is the 8-bit value main returns.
guidedExercise.solution: (1) `U compute(int)` (demangled with `nm -C`), referenced but undefined in main.o. (2) `compute.o` defines `_Z7computei` - `_Z` + `7compute` + `i` for the `int` parameter, shown as `T` by nm. (3) The linker binds the U to the T, main returns `21 * 2 = 42`, and `echo $?` prints **42**.

independentExercise.prompt:
A teammate pastes this into every TU that wants it:

```cpp
const double kTax = 0.07;      // in tax.h, no inline/static keyword
double kFee = 0.02;            // in fee.h
```

Three .cpp files include both headers. (a) Which of the two causes a link error, what is the exact error, and why does the other one not? (b) Give two clean fixes for the problematic declaration. (c) If every TU defines its own copy of the `const` object, what consistency requirement does the ODR still impose on the values?
hints: In C++, namespace-scope const objects default to internal linkage; ordinary variables default to external.
Think about what the linker does when it sees two D symbols with the same name.
independentExercise.solution: (a) `kFee` triggers `multiple definition of 'kFee'`: it has external linkage and each of the three TUs exports a `D kFee` symbol, so the linker sees three definitions. `kTax` is fine because `const` at namespace scope gives internal linkage, each TU gets its own private `d` symbol. (b) Mark it `inline` (`inline double kFee = 0.02;` - one merged definition by ODR), or declare `extern double kFee;` in the header and define it in exactly one .cpp, or (if it should be per-TU) make it `static`. (c) The ODR requires that if the object is *used*, every TU's definition is identical, if one TU had 0.07 and another 0.075, that is an ODR violation with no diagnostic, the silent kind of bug.

commonMistakes: Defining a non-inline function or global variable in a header included by several TUs, each TU exports it and the linker reports 'multiple definition'.
Believing `extern "C"` fixes type/ABI mismatches: it only controls the symbol name, not struct layout or std::string internals.
Confusing `static` locals with `static` globals: a static local is one shared object across all calls; a static global is a per-TU private name.
Assuming mangled names are portable: they are an ABI convention (Itanium on gcc/clang, MSVC uses a different scheme), so never hard-code them.
Fixing 'undefined reference' by re-declaring in a header instead of adding the missing .o/.cpp (or library) to the build.
realWorldApplication: Every shared library, plugin system and C-API wrapper is built on these mechanics: symbol visibility decides what a .so exports, and extern "C" is the contract that lets Python, Rust and vendor binaries call your code.
quantFinanceApplication: A pricing kernel exposed to the desk's Python research environment must publish extern "C" symbols; risk and PnL systems link the same kernel statically and rely on internal-linkage helpers never leaking symbols that collide with another vendor library in the same binary.
summary: A translation unit is one .cpp after preprocessing; the compiler knows nothing beyond it, and the linker resolves each undefined symbol against exactly one definition.
ODR: non-inline external-linkage entities need exactly one program-wide definition; inline functions/templates may repeat but must be token-identical across TUs.
Internal linkage (static, anonymous namespace, const namespace-scope objects) keeps a name private to its TU; nm shows it lowercase (t/d) versus uppercase (T/D/U).
Itanium mangling encodes namespaces and parameter types into symbol names (e.g. _Z7computei); nm -C and c++filt translate them back.
extern "C" emits an unmangled symbol, the door through which dlsym, ctypes and C code enter.

quiz.prompt: Which declaration gives `runs` internal linkage at namespace scope?
quiz.explanation: `static` at namespace scope gives internal linkage: the name is private to the TU. The other three all have external linkage - `extern` is a pure declaration and `inline` variables are still externally visible.
`a` (static) and `b` (anonymous namespace) are internal. `c` and `f` are defined with external linkage, exactly two uppercase nm symbols.

quiz.prompt: What does `extern "C"` actually change about a function declaration?
options: It disables C++ name mangling so the symbol keeps its plain C name
It switches the function to C-style argument evaluation
It makes the function implicitly inline
It gives the function internal linkage
quiz.explanation: It assigns C language linkage: the emitted symbol is unmangled and the block cannot contain overloads. Calling conventions and type safety are unchanged.

quiz.prompt: What does this self-contained program print on stdout?
quiz.explanation: A function-local `static` has static storage duration: there is exactly one `n`, shared by all calls, so the calls see 1, 2, 3.

quiz.prompt: Both a.cpp and b.cpp define `double fee_rate() { return 0.02; }` at namespace scope (not inline). Which rule is violated, what error do you see at which build stage, and name one fix.
quiz.modelAnswer: The One Definition Rule is violated: two definitions of an external-linkage function. The compile stage succeeds; the LINK stage fails with 'multiple definition of fee_rate()'. Fixes: mark it inline, make it static / put it in an anonymous namespace (if per-TU copies are wanted), or define it in one .cpp and declare it extern in the header.
quiz.explanation: Compiling each TU is blind to the other; only the linker sees both T symbols for the same name and refuses. The standard fixes are inline, static/anonymous namespace, or define-once + extern declaration.

quiz.prompt: In nm output, a symbol shown as `U _ZN2fx5priceEdi` means:
options: The symbol is undefined behaviour at runtime
The symbol is a local static variable
The symbol is unique to this object file
This object uses the symbol but does not define it, the linker must resolve it
quiz.explanation: `U` = undefined here: the TU referenced fx::price(double, int) but no definition lives in this object file. If no other object or library defines it, the link fails with 'undefined reference'.

flashcards.front: Internal vs external linkage: and three ways to get internal in C++
flashcards.back: External: linker-visible, other TUs can bind to it. Internal: private to the translation unit. Ways: `static` at namespace scope, anonymous namespace, const namespace-scope variables (non-inline).

flashcards.front: The One Definition Rule in one sentence
flashcards.back: Non-inline external-linkage entities have exactly one program-wide definition; inline functions, templates and class definitions may repeat per TU but must be token-for-token identical (repeats that differ = undefined, usually undiagnosed).

flashcards.front: Mangled name of `int square(int)` under the Itanium ABI?
What does `extern "C"` change (and what does it NOT change)?
flashcards.back: Changes language linkage: symbol emitted unmangled, no overloading in the block. Does NOT change types, layouts or calling safety, a std::string through it is still an ABI risk.
